draft.title: Introductions and thesis statements
card: An introduction is the opening of a text. It orients the reader to the topic, so they know what the text is about.
An introduction also gives a thesis. A thesis is a clear statement of the writer's position or argument.
The rest of the text supports the thesis. Each paragraph should help prove it.
A thesis takes a stand, such as "Homework should be limited to one hour a night." A topic alone, such as "This essay is about homework", is not a thesis.
draft.remember: A good introduction sets up the topic and states a clear position.

a.q: What does a thesis statement do in an introduction?
opts: States the writer's position for the text to support
Lists every piece of evidence the text will use
Tells the reader the topic without taking a side
Retells the story of how the writer chose the topic
a.why: A thesis is the writer's clear position, and the rest of the text supports it. Naming the topic only orients the reader. It does not state a position, so it is not a thesis.
a.clue: The rest of the text has to back it up.

b.q: Which sentence is the best thesis for an essay about school canteens?
opts: Canteens should sell more fruit to help students learn
This essay will talk about what school canteens sell
Many schools in Australia have a canteen for students
What does a canteen sell, and who decides the menu?
b.why: The first sentence takes a clear position and gives a reason the essay can support. The second only announces the topic. The third is a fact and the fourth is a question, so neither states a position.
b.clue: Pick the one that takes a side.

a.best: States the writer's position for the text to support

b.best: Canteens should sell more fruit to help students learn

problems.detail: Why (b) refers to options by position ('The first sentence', 'The second', 'the third', 'the fourth'), but options are shown in random order. As displayed, the first option is the fact and the third is the thesis, so the explanation would point students to the wrong sentences. Refer to each option by its wording instead.
